description: We are a team that wants to share information in a visual way that gets people's attention. We want to do this with video games and comics about the history of space technology.This technology is very important for space knowledge. We don't only want to show its big contribution to human progress. We also want to show its story from the beginning: the first idea, the people who created it together, and some of the trials and errors they made to make it work well.
summary: I made a game called The Forgotten Archive. In the game you travel to the Moon and Mars to find six real NASA machines that everyone forgot about. They are Eagle, the LRRR mirror, the ALSEP battery, Viking 1, Curiosity and Ingenuity. Each level is different and when you find them, they talk to you and tell you who made them and why they were important.We wanted to teach NASA data to kids between 10 and 16 but in a fun way, not just reading numbers. So we made it a game where you feel something for the robots, you don't just memorize data.This is important because kids can see why saving data matters. For example, the little mirror on the Moon that shows the Moon moves 3.8 cm every year, or how Viking made the first map of Mars. Without that old information, the new missions would not be possible. And if we save the data now, they will be the ones who explore space next.
details: The Forgotten Archive is a web video game where you are Inspector Luna. You travel in a cockpit to the Moon or Mars to rescue 6 real NASA machines that were forgotten: Eagle, LRRR, RTG, Viking 1, Curiosity and Ingenuity. Each one is a different mini-game and when you find them, they tell you who created them and why they were important. You can play on PC with arrows and on mobile with a joystick, with music that changes for each planet and with real obstacles on Mars like dust storms and falling rocks.We made it for kids from 10 to 16 years old so they don't just read data, they play it and feel empathy for the robots. This way they understand why NASA data is important, for example that the little LRRR mirror still measures that the Moon moves 3.8 cm every year, or that without Viking's map, Curiosity could not exist.We used HTML5, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas so it works in any browser without installing anything, and we used Google AI Studio (the-forgotten-archive.ai.studio) only as a support tool to make the joystick and collision code faster. The original idea, the research of real NASA data, the story that the Moon is easy and Mars is hard, and the emotional design where each robot is a lonely character, was 100% ours.
dataRefs: Apollo Lunar Modules: The descent stages of the Lunar Modules (like Apollo 11's Eagle) were left behind as launch pads.
Lunar Roving Vehicles (LRVs): Three electric "moon buggies" driven by astronauts. Parked permanently on the Moon.
ALSEP Scientific Packages: Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages (seismometers, retroreflectors, etc.) left to do science after astronauts departed.
Spirit & Opportunity: Twin rovers that operated for years. Both are now inactive monuments to Mars exploration.
Viking 1 & 2 Landers: The first U.S. landers to successfully operate on Mars (1976), remaining exactly where they touched down
Ingenuity Helicopter: The first aircraft on another planet. Sustained rotor damage and became a stationary artifact.
